description: Emprendedor tecnológico e ingeniero full-stack orientado a crear startups de alto impacto. Como cofundador de BattleGraph (EdTech respaldada por Wichay Continental), lidero el desarrollo de plataformas gamificadas con IA, logrando ejecutar pilotos exitosos en el sector educativo. Mi capacidad para validar soluciones ágilmente destaca en retos como la Hackatón del INSN San Borja, IBM Bob 2.0 y Game Jams del MINEDU.
summary: Órbita: La última luz is a 3D browser game for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Your sister vanished with the Aurora expedition; a recovered capsule brings LUMA, an alien creature with a translator, and damaged records. You design each sortie’s suit under a 28 kg limit, choose instruments and explore Earth, a space station, the Moon, Mars and Bennu. The battery pays for life support, movement, instruments, cold, sun and dust; the return reserve is spent only walking home, and leaving radio range triggers a safe recall. The report turns every attempt into a lesson: a battery chart, a decision, result table, a comparison with the previous attempt and one-click proposals. The campaign chains 24 main missions and an evidence chain where collected is not validated. All text and LUMA’s voice are in Spanish and English; science is labelled observation, simplification or fiction; and the game runs with no account, no payments and no online AI.
details:
What it is and how it works. Órbita: La última luz (Orbit: The Last Light) is a 3D exploration and mission-design game that runs directly in the browser. Your sister vanished with the Aurora expedition. Months later a capsule is recovered carrying damaged records and LUMA, an alien creature that communicates through a translator. Your goal is to reconstruct the route, find the survivors and bring them home. The route is Earth and orbit → Moon → Mars → Bennu → return, with resupply at the Martian node.

Each destination is played as a third-person extravehicular sortie. Before leaving you design the suit under a 28 kg limit: battery, thruster, antenna, instruments and one accessory. Mass changes your jump, and instruments unlock or block objectives; a top bar shows what the suit can reach before you leave the lander. uring the sortie the battery pays for life support, walking, dash, double jump, every instrument, cold in shadow, sun on the truss and Martian dust storms. The return reserve can only be spent walking home, and leaving radio range triggers a safe recall: failure never ends the run, it explains it.

The report is the second half of mission design. It shows a battery-over-time chart with objectives, hazards and the moment the reserve was hit; a decision → result table; a comparison with the previous attempt; and up to three concrete proposals, always within the mass limit, loadable with one click. The campaign chains 24 main missions across four chapters. On the Moon the three archive pieces can be recovered in any order; Mars adds a habitat, a valley, a relay and a power failure; Bennu uses anchored contact and limited speed. The AUR-E01–AUR-E07 evidence chain separates collected from validated: an unauthenticated piece never reveals the next destination. The ending requires the full survivor manifest and reserves for the return trip.

Benefits and impact. The game turns mission design into a decision you can feel: it teaches trade-offs between mass, power, time, science and safety, and shows that failure can be informative. It needs no prior orbital knowledge, no account, no payments and no online AI, and it saves in the browser. It can serve classrooms, science clubs and museums as a practical introduction to the mission lifecycle, while its story — including a definitive ending for LUMA — gives an emotional reason to care about the numbers.

Creativity. The mission is the narrative: engineering opens clues and clues change engineering. LUMA is not a rover but an alien animal with a translator, a stellar palette that evolves by chapter and deterministic abilities that help without replacing the player. The report doubles as teaching material, and the “Science: model and reality” screen labels every mechanic as observation, simplification or fiction, with NASA links.

Tools. TypeScript, three.js 0.187 on WebGL with a custom fixed-step loop and a kinematic controller over height fields, no physics engine; React 19 and Zustand for the HUD and menus; Zod for validating data and saves; Dexie and IndexedDB for transactional saves; Vite and Node 24 with pnpm; code-generated art, geometry, textures, sky and audio; baked lighting, quality tiers and post-processing; node:test and Playwright (101 rule tests and 35 recorded Chrome walkthroughs); Vercel for publishing. Phaser is kept only for the legacy 2D prototype.

Factors considered. Hackathon eligibility — research and documentation before the start, implementation only during the event; a 3 person team supported by coding agents; zero budget and no charges; modest hardware (Intel Iris Xe), with automatic quality and a usable low tier; single player and short sessions; Spanish and

English text, subtitles and LUMA voice clips; accessibility with labels and symbols, keyboard focus, reduced motion and fullscreen; traceable science, no secrets or personal data; MIT for code and CC BY 4.0 for original documentation and content.
